blocks.tex: These exercises are extra credit: none of them is a gate, and the chapter clears on its theorems alone. Take them in any order; each may use anything proved in the chapter, and a few of the later ones lean on earlier exercises, which are then named in their hints.

blocks.title: Zero sets are invisible
blocks.tex:
Let $Z \subseteq \R^n$ be a zero set and let $A \subseteq \R^n$ be arbitrary. Show that
\[ m^*(A \cup Z) = m^*A = m^*(A \setminus Z), \]
and that $A \cup Z$ is measurable if and only if $A$ is measurable.
blocks.proof:
By monotonicity, $m^*(A \setminus Z) \le m^*A \le m^*(A \cup Z)$. By countable subadditivity, $m^*(A \cup Z) \le m^*A + m^*Z = m^*A$. Also $A = (A \setminus Z) \cup (A \cap Z)$ with $A \cap Z \subseteq Z$, so
\[ m^*A \le m^*(A \setminus Z) + m^*(A \cap Z) \le m^*(A \setminus Z) + m^*Z = m^*(A \setminus Z). \]
Hence the three outer measures are equal.

Zero sets are measurable. If $A$ is measurable, then $A \cup Z$ is the union of two measurable sets, hence measurable. Conversely suppose $A \cup Z$ is measurable. The set $Z \setminus A$ is a subset of the zero set $Z$, hence a zero set, hence measurable, and
\[ A = (A \cup Z) \setminus (Z \setminus A), \]
a difference of two measurable sets, so $A$ is measurable.
hints: Monotonicity and subadditivity give the equalities. For measurability, write $A$ in terms of $A \cup Z$ and a subset of $Z$.

blocks.title: A fat Cantor set
blocks.tex:
Let $K^0 = [0,1]$. For $k \ge 1$ obtain $K^k$ from $K^{k-1}$ by removing from each of the $2^{k-1}$ closed intervals making up $K^{k-1}$ the open interval of length $4^{-k}$ centred at its midpoint, so that $K^k$ is the union of $2^k$ pairwise disjoint closed intervals. Let $K = \bigcap_{k \ge 0} K^k$.

(a) Show that the construction is possible (the removed interval is shorter than the interval it is removed from), that all intervals of $K^k$ have the same length $L_k \le 2^{-k}$, and that $K$ is closed.

(b) Show that $mK = \tfrac12$.

(c) Show that $K$ contains no interval of positive length.

So a closed subset of $\R$ can have positive measure and empty interior.
blocks.proof:
(a) We show by induction on $k$ that the $2^k$ intervals of $K^k$ all have the same length $L_k = 2^{-k-1}(1 + 2^{-k})$, and that the construction of $K^k$ is possible. For $k = 0$, $L_0 = 2^{-1} \cdot 2 = 1$. Suppose the claim holds for $k - 1$, where $k \ge 1$. Then $L_{k-1} = 2^{-k}(1 + 2^{1-k}) > 2^{-k} > 4^{-k}$, so an open interval of length $4^{-k}$ centred at the midpoint of an interval of length $L_{k-1}$ lies strictly inside it, and removing it leaves two disjoint closed intervals of the same length
\[ L_k = \frac{L_{k-1} - 4^{-k}}{2} = 2^{-k-1}\bigl( 1 + 2^{1-k} - 2^{-k} \bigr) = 2^{-k-1}\bigl( 1 + 2^{-k} \bigr). \]
Intervals coming from different intervals of $K^{k-1}$ are disjoint because their parents are. Since $1 + 2^{-k} \le 2$, $L_k \le 2^{-k}$. Each $K^k$ is a finite union of closed intervals, hence closed, and $K$ is an intersection of closed sets, hence closed.

(b) Each $K^k$ is a finite union of pairwise disjoint boxes, hence measurable, and by finite additivity and the measure of a box, $mK^k = 2^k L_k = \tfrac12 + 2^{-k-1}$. The sets $K^k$ decrease, $mK^0 = 1 < \infty$, and $K = \bigcap_k K^k$, so by downward measure continuity
\[ mK = \lim_{k \to \infty} \Bigl( \tfrac12 + 2^{-k-1} \Bigr) = \tfrac12. \]

(c) Suppose $I \subseteq K$ is an interval of positive length and pick $a < b$ in $I$. Then $[a,b] \subseteq K \subseteq K^k$ for every $k$. Choose $k$ with $2^{-k} < b - a$ and write $K^k = J_1 \cup \dots \cup J_{2^k}$ with the $J_i$ pairwise disjoint closed intervals. Then $[a,b]$ is the union of the pairwise disjoint sets $[a,b] \cap J_i$, each of which is closed. If two of them were nonempty, $[a,b]$ would be the union of two disjoint nonempty closed sets (one piece and the union of the remaining pieces, which is closed as a finite union of closed sets), contradicting the connectedness of the interval $[a,b]$ (Chapter 2). So $[a,b] \subseteq J_i$ for a single $i$, which is impossible since $\abs{J_i} = L_k \le 2^{-k} < b - a$. Hence $K$ contains no interval of positive length.
hints: Keep track of the common length $L_k$ of the intervals of $K^k$: $L_k = (L_{k-1} - 4^{-k})/2$. Guess and verify a closed formula.
$mK^k = 2^k L_k$, and the removed lengths form a geometric series with sum $\tfrac12$. Use downward measure continuity.
An interval inside $K$ lies inside $K^k$ for every $k$; by connectedness it lies inside a single piece of $K^k$, which is shorter than $2^{-k}$.

blocks.title: Fatou for sets, and the Borel–Cantelli lemma
blocks.tex:
Let $E_1, E_2, \dots$ be measurable subsets of $\R^n$. Put
\[ \liminf_{k} E_k = \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty \bigcap_{j \ge k} E_j, \qquad \limsup_{k} E_k = \bigcap_{k=1}^\infty \bigcup_{j \ge k} E_j ; \]
the first is the set of points lying in all but finitely many of the $E_j$, the second the set of points lying in infinitely many of them.

(a) Show that both sets are measurable and that $m\bigl( \liminf_k E_k \bigr) \le \liminf_k mE_k$.

(b) Show that if $\sum_{k} mE_k < \infty$, then $\limsup_k E_k$ is a zero set: almost every point of $\R^n$ lies in only finitely many of the $E_k$.
blocks.proof:
Measurable sets form a $\sigma$-algebra, so the sets $F_k = \bigcap_{j \ge k} E_j$ and $G_k = \bigcup_{j \ge k} E_j$ are measurable, and so are $\liminf_k E_k = \bigcup_k F_k$ and $\limsup_k E_k = \bigcap_k G_k$.

(a) The sets $F_k$ increase with $k$, so by upward measure continuity $m(\liminf_k E_k) = \lim_k mF_k$. For every $j \ge k$ we have $F_k \subseteq E_j$, hence $mF_k \le mE_j$ by monotonicity, and so $mF_k \le \inf_{j \ge k} mE_j$. The right side increases with $k$ to $\liminf_k mE_k$, and limits preserve weak inequalities, so $\lim_k mF_k \le \liminf_k mE_k$.

(b) For every $k$, countable subadditivity gives $mG_k \le \sum_{j \ge k} mE_j$, the tail of a convergent series, which tends to $0$ as $k \to \infty$. Since $\limsup_k E_k \subseteq G_k$ for every $k$, monotonicity gives $m(\limsup_k E_k) \le mG_k$ for every $k$, hence $m(\limsup_k E_k) = 0$. The set of points lying in infinitely many $E_k$ is thus a zero set, which is the statement about almost every point.
hints: The sets $\bigcap_{j \ge k} E_j$ increase with $k$; use upward measure continuity and compare each with the $E_j$ it sits inside.
For (b), $\bigcup_{j \ge k} E_j$ has measure at most the tail $\sum_{j \ge k} mE_j$, and the upper limit set lies inside it for every $k$.

blocks.title: Boxes suffice as test sets
blocks.tex:
Show that a set $A \subseteq \R^n$ is measurable if and only if
\[ \abs{B} = m^*(A \cap B) + m^*(B \setminus A) \]
for every box $B \subseteq \R^n$.
blocks.proof:
If $A$ is measurable, the displayed equation is Carathéodory's condition with the test set $X = B$, because $m^*B = \abs{B}$ and $B \cap A^c = B \setminus A$.

Conversely suppose the equation holds for every box. Fix a box $B$ and consider the subset $A \cap B$ of $B$. Since $B \setminus (A \cap B) = B \setminus A$, the hypothesis says exactly that $\abs{B} = m^*(A \cap B) + m^*(B \setminus (A \cap B))$, that is, $A \cap B$ divides $B$ cleanly. By the corollary on subsets of a box, $A \cap B$ is measurable. Taking $B = C_k = [-k,k]^n$ for $k \in \N$, the set $A = \bigcup_k (A \cap C_k)$ is a countable union of measurable sets, hence measurable.
hints: Apply the corollary that a subset of a box is measurable if and only if it divides the box cleanly to the set $A \cap B$, then exhaust $\R^n$ by boxes.

blocks.title: A measurable set is nearly a finite union of boxes
blocks.tex:
Let $E \subseteq \R^n$ with $m^*E < \infty$. Show that $E$ is measurable if and only if for every $\eps > 0$ there is a finite union $F$ of boxes with
\[ m^*(E \,\triangle\, F) < \eps, \qquad \text{where } E \,\triangle\, F = (E \setminus F) \cup (F \setminus E). \]
(This is the first of Littlewood's three principles: every measurable set of finite measure is nearly a finite union of boxes.)
blocks.proof:
\emph{Measurable $\Rightarrow$ nearly a finite union of boxes.} Let $E$ be measurable and $\eps > 0$. By regularity there is an open set $U \supseteq E$ with $m(U \setminus E) < \eps/2$, and then $mU = mE + m(U \setminus E) < \infty$ because $mE = m^*E < \infty$. By the lemma on open sets, $U = \bigcup_{k} B_k$ for open boxes $B_1, B_2, \dots$. Let $F_N = B_1 \cup \dots \cup B_N$; these are measurable sets, they increase with $N$, and their union is $U$. By upward measure continuity $mF_N \to mU$, and since $mU < \infty$ and $F_N \subseteq U$, $m(U \setminus F_N) = mU - mF_N \to 0$. Choose $N$ with $m(U \setminus F_N) < \eps/2$ and put $F = F_N$. Then $E \setminus F \subseteq U \setminus F$ and $F \setminus E \subseteq U \setminus E$, so by subadditivity and monotonicity
\[ m^*(E \,\triangle\, F) \le m(U \setminus F) + m(U \setminus E) < \eps. \]

\emph{Nearly a finite union of boxes $\Rightarrow$ measurable.} Let $X \subseteq \R^n$ be a test set with $m^*X < \infty$, let $\eps > 0$, and let $F$ be a finite union of boxes with $m^*(E \,\triangle\, F) < \eps$. The set $F$ is measurable. Every point of $X \cap E$ lies in $X \cap F$ or in $E \setminus F$, and every point of $X \cap E^c$ lies in $X \cap F^c$ or in $F \setminus E$:
\[ X \cap E \subseteq (X \cap F) \cup (E \setminus F), \qquad X \cap E^c \subseteq (X \cap F^c) \cup (F \setminus E). \]
By subadditivity, then the measurability of $F$ with test set $X$ and monotonicity ($E \setminus F$ and $F \setminus E$ are subsets of $E \,\triangle\, F$),
\[ m^*(X \cap E) + m^*(X \cap E^c) \le m^*(X \cap F) + m^*(X \cap F^c) + m^*(E \setminus F) + m^*(F \setminus E) \le m^*X + 2\eps. \]
As $\eps > 0$ is arbitrary, $m^*(X \cap E) + m^*(X \cap E^c) \le m^*X$, which is the inequality that needs checking. Hence $E$ is measurable. (This direction did not use $m^*E < \infty$.)
hints: For a measurable $E$, regularity gives an open $U \supseteq E$ of finite measure with $m(U \setminus E)$ small. An open set is a countable union of open boxes, and finitely many of them already fill up most of $U$: use upward measure continuity.
For the converse, test $E$ against a set $X$ by comparing with $F$: $X \cap E \subseteq (X \cap F) \cup (E \setminus F)$, and similarly for the complements.
Only the half-condition is needed: $m^*(X \cap E) + m^*(X \cap E^c) \le m^*X + 2\eps$ for every $\eps > 0$.

blocks.title: Outer measure is continuous from below
blocks.tex:
Let $A_1 \subseteq A_2 \subseteq \cdots$ be subsets of $\R^n$, measurable or not. Show that
\[ m^*\Bigl( \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty A_k \Bigr) = \lim_{k \to \infty} m^*A_k . \]
blocks.proof:
Let $A = \bigcup_k A_k$. By monotonicity $m^*A_k \le m^*A_{k+1} \le m^*A$ for every $k$, so the limit $L = \lim_k m^*A_k$ exists in $[0, \infty]$ and $L \le m^*A$.

For the reverse inequality choose for each $k$ a hull $H_k$ of $A_k$: a measurable set with $H_k \supseteq A_k$ and $mH_k = m^*A_k$. The hulls need not increase, so put
\[ H_k' = \bigcap_{j \ge k} H_j . \]
Each $H_k'$ is measurable. Since $A_k \subseteq A_j \subseteq H_j$ for all $j \ge k$, we have $A_k \subseteq H_k'$; and $H_k' \subseteq H_k$. Hence $m^*A_k \le mH_k' \le mH_k = m^*A_k$, so $mH_k' = m^*A_k$. The sets $H_k'$ increase with $k$ (fewer sets are intersected), and their union $H'$ contains $\bigcup_k A_k = A$. By monotonicity and upward measure continuity,
\[ m^*A \le mH' = \lim_{k \to \infty} mH_k' = \lim_{k \to \infty} m^*A_k = L . \]
hints: Replace each $A_k$ by a measurable hull. Measure continuity needs increasing sets, and the hulls need not increase.
$\bigcap_{j \ge k} H_j$ is still a hull of $A_k$, and these sets do increase with $k$.

blocks.title: A measurable set adds to both measures
blocks.tex:
Let $E \subseteq \R^n$ be measurable and let $A \subseteq \R^n$ be an arbitrary set with $A \cap E = \emptyset$. Show that
\[ m^*(A \cup E) = m^*A + mE \qquad \text{and} \qquad m_*(A \cup E) = m_*A + mE . \]
blocks.proof:
\emph{Outer measure.} Carathéodory's condition for $E$ with the test set $X = A \cup E$ reads $m^*(A \cup E) = m^*((A \cup E) \cap E) + m^*((A \cup E) \cap E^c)$. Since $A \cap E = \emptyset$, the two pieces are $E$ and $A$, so $m^*(A \cup E) = m^*E + m^*A = mE + m^*A$.

\emph{Inner measure, $\ge$.} Let $K \subseteq A$ and $K' \subseteq E$ be closed. Then $K \cup K'$ is a closed subset of $A \cup E$, and $K$, $K'$ are disjoint measurable sets, so by the definition of inner measure and finite additivity
\[ m_*(A \cup E) \ge m(K \cup K') = mK + mK' . \]
Taking the supremum over closed $K' \subseteq E$ gives $m_*(A \cup E) \ge mK + m_*E = mK + mE$, because $m_*E = mE$ for measurable $E$ (if $mE = \infty$ the right side is $\infty$ and the inequality says $m_*(A \cup E) = \infty$). Taking the supremum over closed $K \subseteq A$ gives $m_*(A \cup E) \ge m_*A + mE$.

\emph{Inner measure, $\le$.} Let $K \subseteq A \cup E$ be closed. It is measurable, and $K = (K \cap E) \sqcup (K \setminus E)$, so $mK = m(K \cap E) + m(K \setminus E)$. Here $m(K \cap E) \le mE$ by monotonicity. The set $K \setminus E$ is measurable and, since $A \cap E = \emptyset$, it is contained in $A$; by the first properties of inner measure, $m(K \setminus E) = m_*(K \setminus E) \le m_*A$. Thus $mK \le mE + m_*A$ for every closed $K \subseteq A \cup E$, and taking the supremum, $m_*(A \cup E) \le m_*A + mE$.
hints: For outer measure, $A \cup E$ itself is a test set for $E$.
For inner measure, a closed subset of $A \cup E$ splits along $E$ into two measurable pieces; the piece inside $A$ is measurable, so its measure equals its inner measure, which is at most $m_*A$.

blocks.title: Inner measure by compact sets
blocks.tex:
Show that for every $A \subseteq \R^n$,
\[ m_*A = \sup \set{ mK : K \subseteq A, \ K \text{ compact} }. \]
Deduce that every measurable set $E$ with $mE > 0$ contains a compact set $K$ with $0 < mK < \infty$.
blocks.proof:
Compact subsets of $\R^n$ are closed (Chapter 2), so the supremum over compact subsets of $A$ is taken over a subfamily of the closed subsets of $A$, and is at most $m_*A$.

Conversely let $K \subseteq A$ be closed and put $K_j = K \cap [-j,j]^n$ for $j \in \N$. Each $K_j$ is closed and bounded, hence compact by the Heine–Borel theorem, and $K_j \subseteq A$. The sets $K_j$ increase with $j$ and their union is $K$, so by upward measure continuity $mK = \lim_j mK_j$, which is at most the supremum over compact subsets of $A$. Taking the supremum over closed $K \subseteq A$ gives $m_*A \le \sup \set{mK : K \subseteq A \text{ compact}}$.

If $E$ is measurable with $mE > 0$, then $m_*E = mE > 0$, so by what was just shown some compact $K \subseteq E$ has $mK > 0$. A compact set is bounded, so it lies in a box, and $mK$ is at most the volume of that box, hence finite.
hints: A closed set is the increasing union of the compact sets $K \cap [-j,j]^n$; use upward measure continuity.

blocks.title: Every set of positive outer measure contains a nonmeasurable set
blocks.tex: Let $A \subseteq \R$ with $m^*A > 0$. Show that $A$ has a subset that is not Lebesgue measurable. (The remark closing the section on regularity states this without proof.)
blocks.proof:
\emph{Step 1: reduction to $A \subseteq [0,1)$.} The sets $A_j = A \cap [j, j+1)$, $j \in \Z$, are countably many and their union is $A$. If every $A_j$ were a zero set, so would be $A$; hence $m^*A_j > 0$ for some $j$. Translations are meseometries, so the set $A' = A_j - j \subseteq [0,1)$ has $m^*A' = m^*A_j > 0$, and if $S' \subseteq A'$ is not measurable then neither is $S = S' + j \subseteq A_j \subseteq A$: were $S$ measurable, $S' = S - j$ would be measurable too. So it suffices to treat $A' $, and we rename it $A$, assuming from now on $A \subseteq [0,1)$ and $m^*A > 0$.

\emph{Step 2: a measurable subset of a translate of the Vitali set is a zero set.} Let $V \subseteq [0,1)$ be the Vitali set, let $q_1, q_2, \dots$ enumerate $\Q \cap (-1,1)$, and let $V_k = V + q_k$. Recall from the proof of Vitali's theorem that the $V_k$ are pairwise disjoint, cover $[0,1)$, and lie in $(-1, 2)$. Suppose $W \subseteq V_k$ is measurable. Then $W' = W - q_k \subseteq V$ is measurable with $mW' = mW$, and for every $j$ the translate $W' + q_j \subseteq V_j$ is measurable with measure $mW'$. These translates are pairwise disjoint, being subsets of the pairwise disjoint sets $V_j$, and they all lie in $(-1, 2)$. By countable additivity and monotonicity,
\[ \sum_{j=1}^\infty mW' = m\Bigl( \bigsqcup_j (W' + q_j) \Bigr) \le m(-1,2) = 3, \]
which forces $mW' = 0$. Hence $mW = 0$.

\emph{Step 3.} Since the $V_k$ cover $[0,1) \supseteq A$, we have $A = \bigcup_k (A \cap V_k)$. If every $A \cap V_k$ were measurable, each would be a zero set by Step 2, and $A$ would be a countable union of zero sets, hence a zero set, contradicting $m^*A > 0$. Therefore some $A \cap V_k$ is a nonmeasurable subset of $A$.
hints: Reduce to $A \subseteq [0,1)$: some piece $A \cap [j,j+1)$ has positive outer measure, and translation changes nothing.
Cut $A$ along the translates $V_k = V + q_k$ of the Vitali set, which partition $[0,1)$.
A measurable subset of $V_k$ has measure zero: translate it back into $V$ and rerun the disjoint-translates argument from Vitali's proof. Then $A$ would be a countable union of zero sets.

blocks.title: The difference set of a set of positive measure (Steinhaus)
blocks.tex: Let $E \subseteq \R^n$ be measurable with $mE > 0$. Show that there is a $\delta > 0$ such that every $v \in \R^n$ with $\abs{v} < \delta$ can be written as $v = x - y$ with $x, y \in E$. In other words, the difference set $E - E = \set{x - y : x, y \in E}$ contains an open ball about the origin.
blocks.proof:
\emph{Step 1: a compact piece.} By the exercise on inner measure by compact sets, there is a compact $K \subseteq E$ with $0 < mK < \infty$. Since $K - K \subseteq E - E$, it suffices to prove the claim for $K$.

\emph{Step 2: a tight open neighbourhood.} Outer measure is computed by open sets and $m^*K = mK < \infty$, so there is an open set $U \supseteq K$ with $mU < mK + mK = 2\,mK$.

\emph{Step 3: small translates of $K$ stay inside $U$.} We claim there is a $\delta > 0$ such that $K + v \subseteq U$ whenever $\abs{v} < \delta$. If not, then for every $j \in \N$ there are $v_j$ with $\abs{v_j} < 1/j$ and $x_j \in K$ with $x_j + v_j \notin U$. Since $K$ is compact, a subsequence $x_{j_i}$ converges to some $x \in K$ (Chapter 2). Then $x_{j_i} + v_{j_i} \to x$ because $v_{j_i} \to 0$. But $x \in K \subseteq U$ and $U$ is open, so $x_{j_i} + v_{j_i} \in U$ for all large $i$, a contradiction.

\emph{Step 4: two translates must meet.} Let $\abs{v} < \delta$. Translations are meseometries, so $K + v$ is measurable with $m(K + v) = mK$, and $K \cup (K + v) \subseteq U$. If $K$ and $K + v$ were disjoint, finite additivity would give $m(K \cup (K+v)) = 2\,mK$, whereas monotonicity gives $m(K \cup (K+v)) \le mU < 2\,mK$. So there is a point $x \in K \cap (K + v)$: $x \in K$ and $x = y + v$ with $y \in K$, whence $v = x - y \in K - K \subseteq E - E$.
hints: Shrink $E$ to a compact $K$ with $0 < mK < \infty$ (an earlier exercise), then enclose $K$ in an open $U$ with $mU < 2\,mK$.
Compactness gives a $\delta > 0$ such that $K + v \subseteq U$ for every $\abs{v} < \delta$: argue by contradiction with a convergent subsequence.
Two translates of $K$, both inside $U$, have total measure $2\,mK > mU$, so they cannot be disjoint.

blocks.title: Curves have no area
blocks.tex:
(a) Let $\gamma : [0,1] \to \R^2$ be Lipschitz with constant $L$, that is, $\abs{\gamma(s) - \gamma(t)} \le L\abs{s - t}$ for all $s, t \in [0,1]$. Show that $\gamma([0,1])$ is a zero set in $\R^2$.

(b) Let $f : [a,b] \to \R$ be continuous. Show that its graph $\set{ (x, f(x)) : x \in [a,b] }$ is a zero set in $\R^2$.
blocks.proof:
(a) Fix $N \in \N$ and split $[0,1]$ into the $N$ closed intervals $I_r = [t_r, t_r + 1/N]$ with $t_r = (r-1)/N$, $r = 1, \dots, N$. For $s \in I_r$, $\abs{\gamma(s) - \gamma(t_r)} \le L\abs{s - t_r} \le L/N$, so each of the two coordinates of $\gamma(s) - \gamma(t_r)$ has absolute value at most $L/N$. Hence $\gamma(I_r)$ lies in the closed square $Q_r$ centred at $\gamma(t_r)$ with side $2L/N$, whose area is $4L^2/N^2$. The $N$ squares $Q_r$ cover $\gamma([0,1])$, and since any boxes may be used in coverings,
\[ m^*\gamma([0,1]) \le N \cdot \frac{4L^2}{N^2} = \frac{4L^2}{N}. \]
As $N$ is arbitrary, $m^*\gamma([0,1]) = 0$.

(b) The function $f$ is continuous on the compact interval $[a,b]$, hence uniformly continuous (Chapter 2). Let $\eps > 0$ and choose $\delta > 0$ such that $\abs{f(x) - f(x')} < \eps$ whenever $x, x' \in [a,b]$ and $\abs{x - x'} < \delta$. Choose $N \in \N$ with $(b-a)/N < \delta$ and split $[a,b]$ into $N$ closed intervals $I_r$ of length $(b-a)/N$, with left endpoints $x_r$. For $x \in I_r$ we have $\abs{x - x_r} < \delta$, so $\abs{f(x) - f(x_r)} < \eps$, and the point $(x, f(x))$ lies in the box $I_r \times [f(x_r) - \eps, f(x_r) + \eps]$ of area $2\eps(b-a)/N$. These $N$ boxes cover the graph, so
\[ m^*\set{(x, f(x)) : x \in [a,b]} \le N \cdot \frac{2\eps(b-a)}{N} = 2\eps(b-a). \]
As $\eps$ is arbitrary, the graph is a zero set.
hints: Cut the parameter interval into $N$ equal pieces; the image of each piece fits in a small square, and the total area of the squares tends to $0$.
For a continuous $f$, uniform continuity makes the graph over a short interval fit inside a short, thin box.

blocks.title: A meseomorphism that is not Lipschitz
blocks.tex:
(a) Let $T : \R^n \to \R^n$ be continuous, and suppose $TZ$ is a zero set for every zero set $Z \subseteq \R^n$. Show that $TE$ is measurable for every measurable $E \subseteq \R^n$.

(b) Show that $T(x) = x^3$ is a meseomorphism of $\R$, although neither $T$ nor $T^{-1}$ is Lipschitz on $\R$.
blocks.proof:
(a) Let $E$ be measurable. By the theorem on $F_\sigma$-sets, $E = \bigcup_j K_j \cup Z$ with each $K_j$ closed and $Z$ a zero set. With $C_i = [-i,i]^n$, each $K_j \cap C_i$ is closed and bounded, hence compact by the Heine–Borel theorem, and $K_j = \bigcup_i (K_j \cap C_i)$. Since $T$ is continuous, $T(K_j \cap C_i)$ is compact, hence closed, hence measurable. By hypothesis $TZ$ is a zero set, hence measurable. So
\[ TE = \bigcup_{i,j} T(K_j \cap C_i) \;\cup\; TZ \]
is a countable union of measurable sets, and is measurable.

(b) The map $T(x) = x^3$ is a continuous bijection of $\R$ whose inverse $S(y) = y^{1/3}$ (the real cube root, with $S(-y) = -S(y)$) is continuous. By (a) applied to $T$ and to $S$, it suffices to show that both send zero sets to zero sets.

\emph{$T$.} For $x, y \in [-k,k]$, $\abs{x^3 - y^3} = \abs{x - y}\,\abs{x^2 + xy + y^2} \le 3k^2 \abs{x - y}$, so the restriction of $T$ to $[-k,k]$ is Lipschitz. If $Z$ is a zero set, then $Z \cap [-k,k]$ is a zero set and, since Lipschitz maps do not inflate zero sets, $T(Z \cap [-k,k])$ is a zero set. Hence $TZ = \bigcup_k T(Z \cap [-k,k])$ is a countable union of zero sets, hence a zero set.

\emph{$S$.} For $u, v \in [1/k, k]$ put $a = S(u)$, $b = S(v)$; then $a, b \ge k^{-1/3}$, so $a^2 + ab + b^2 \ge 3k^{-2/3}$, and
\[ \abs{S(u) - S(v)} = \abs{a - b} = \frac{\abs{a^3 - b^3}}{a^2 + ab + b^2} \le \frac{k^{2/3}}{3}\, \abs{u - v} \]
(trivially if $a = b$). So $S$ is Lipschitz on $[1/k, k]$, and by the symmetry $S(-y) = -S(y)$ also on $[-k, -1/k]$ with the same constant. Since $\R = \set{0} \cup \bigcup_k \bigl( [1/k, k] \cup [-k, -1/k] \bigr)$, for a zero set $Z$ the image $SZ$ is contained in $\set{S(0)} \cup \bigcup_k \bigl( S(Z \cap [1/k,k]) \cup S(Z \cap [-k,-1/k]) \bigr)$, a countable union of zero sets (a single point and Lipschitz images of zero sets). Hence $SZ$ is a zero set.

Therefore $T$ and $T^{-1} = S$ both send measurable sets to measurable sets, and $T$ is a meseomorphism. Finally, $\abs{T(x) - T(0)} / \abs{x - 0} = x^2$ is unbounded, and $\abs{S(y) - S(0)} / \abs{y - 0} = \abs{y}^{-2/3}$ is unbounded as $y \to 0$, so neither map is Lipschitz on $\R$.
hints: Reread the proof that Lipschitz maps preserve measurability: the Lipschitz condition is used only to control the zero set in $E = \bigcup_j K_j \cup Z$.

$x \mapsto x^3$ is Lipschitz on each $[-k,k]$, and the cube root is Lipschitz on each $[1/k,k]$ and $[-k,-1/k]$. A zero set is the countable union of its pieces in these intervals, plus possibly the origin.

blocks.title: Translating and dilating the integrand
blocks.tex:
Let $f : \R^n \to [0, \infty]$ be measurable, $v \in \R^n$, and $\lambda \ne 0$. Show that the functions $x \mapsto f(x + v)$ and $x \mapsto f(\lambda x)$ are measurable, with
\[ \int f(x + v)\, dx = \int f \qquad \text{and} \qquad \int f(\lambda x)\, dx = \abs{\lambda}^{-n} \int f . \]
blocks.proof:
Let $g(x) = f(x + v)$. For $(x, y) \in \R^n \times \R$,
\[ (x, y) \in \mathcal{U}g \iff 0 \le y < f(x + v) \iff (x + v, y) \in \mathcal{U}f \iff (x, y) \in \tau_w(\mathcal{U}f), \]
where $\tau_w$ is the translation of $\R^{n+1}$ by $w = (-v, 0)$, since $(x,y) = (x+v, y) + w$ and $\tau_w$ is a bijection. So $\mathcal{U}g = \tau_w(\mathcal{U}f)$. Translations are meseometries, so $\mathcal{U}g$ is measurable with $m(\mathcal{U}g) = m(\mathcal{U}f)$; that is, $g$ is measurable and $\int g = \int f$.

Let $h(x) = f(\lambda x)$ and let $D : \R^{n+1} \to \R^{n+1}$ be the diagonal map $D(x, y) = (\lambda x, y)$, with factors $\lambda$ ($n$ times) and $1$. Then
\[ (x, y) \in \mathcal{U}h \iff 0 \le y < f(\lambda x) \iff D(x, y) \in \mathcal{U}f \iff (x, y) \in D^{-1}(\mathcal{U}f). \]
The inverse $D^{-1}$ is the diagonal map with factors $1/\lambda$ ($n$ times) and $1$; by the theorem on diagonal maps it is a meseomorphism that multiplies measure by $\abs{1/\lambda}^n = \abs{\lambda}^{-n}$. Hence $\mathcal{U}h = D^{-1}(\mathcal{U}f)$ is measurable and $\int h = \abs{\lambda}^{-n}\, m(\mathcal{U}f) = \abs{\lambda}^{-n} \int f$.
hints: Express the undergraph of the new function as the image of $\mathcal{U}f$ under a translation, or under a diagonal map, of $\R^{n+1}$.

blocks.title: Truncation
blocks.tex:
Let $f : \R^n \to [0, \infty]$ be measurable. For $k \in \N$ let $C_k = [-k,k]^n$ and define $f_k = \min(f, k)\, \chi_{C_k}$, that is, $f_k(x) = \min(f(x), k)$ for $x \in C_k$ and $f_k(x) = 0$ otherwise. Show that each $f_k$ is measurable, that $\int f_k \le k (2k)^n < \infty$, and that
\[ \int f = \lim_{k \to \infty} \int f_k . \]
blocks.proof:
For $a \ge 0$, the superlevel set $\set{f_k > a}$ equals $\set{f > a} \cap C_k$ if $a < k$ and is empty if $a \ge k$. The set $\set{f > a}$ is measurable by the theorem on superlevel sets and $C_k$ is a box, so $\set{f_k > a}$ is measurable for every $a \ge 0$, and $f_k$ is measurable by the same theorem.

Since $f_k \le k\chi_{C_k}$, a simple function, monotonicity of the integral gives $\int f_k \le k\, mC_k = k(2k)^n$.

The sequence is increasing: if $x \notin C_{k+1}$ then $f_k(x) = f_{k+1}(x) = 0$; if $x \in C_{k+1} \setminus C_k$ then $f_k(x) = 0 \le f_{k+1}(x)$; and if $x \in C_k$ then $f_k(x) = \min(f(x), k) \le \min(f(x), k+1) = f_{k+1}(x)$. It converges pointwise to $f$: given $x$, for all large $k$ we have $x \in C_k$, and then $f_k(x) = \min(f(x), k)$, which equals $f(x)$ once $k \ge f(x)$ if $f(x) < \infty$, and equals $k$, tending to $\infty = f(x)$, if $f(x) = \infty$. By the monotone convergence theorem, $\int f_k \to \int f$.
hints: Compute the superlevel sets of $f_k$, then apply monotone convergence.

blocks.title: The integral as a supremum over simple functions
blocks.tex:
Let $f : \R^n \to [0, \infty]$ be measurable. Show that
\[ \int f = \sup \set{ \int \varphi : \varphi \text{ simple}, \ \varphi \le f } . \]
(This is the usual textbook definition of the Lebesgue integral of a nonnegative function.)
blocks.proof:
If $\varphi$ is simple with $\varphi \le f$, then $\varphi$ is measurable by the proposition on integrals of simple functions, and $\int \varphi \le \int f$ by monotonicity of the integral. So the supremum is at most $\int f$.

Conversely, the approximation lemma gives simple functions $\varphi_1 \le \varphi_2 \le \cdots$ with $\varphi_k(x) \to f(x)$ for every $x$. Each $\varphi_k \le f$, since $\varphi_k(x) \le \varphi_j(x)$ for all $j \ge k$ and $\varphi_j(x) \to f(x)$. By the monotone convergence theorem $\int \varphi_k \to \int f$, so the supremum is at least $\int f$.
hints: One inequality is monotonicity of the integral; the other is the approximation lemma together with monotone convergence.

blocks.title: The integral over a set is countably additive
blocks.tex:
Let $f : \R^n \to [0, \infty]$ be measurable, and for measurable $E \subseteq \R^n$ write $\int_E f = \int f\chi_E$.

(a) If $E_1, E_2, \dots$ are pairwise disjoint measurable sets with union $E$, then $\int_E f = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \int_{E_k} f$.

(b) If $E_1 \subseteq E_2 \subseteq \cdots$ are measurable sets with union $E$, then $\int_{E_k} f \to \int_E f$.

(c) If $Z \subseteq \R^n$ is a zero set, then $\int_Z f = 0$.
blocks.proof:
For measurable $E$ the function $f\chi_E$ is measurable, because $\set{f\chi_E > a} = \set{f > a} \cap E$ for every $a \ge 0$ (as noted in the definition of the integral of a function of arbitrary sign).

(a) For every $x$, at most one of the numbers $\chi_{E_k}(x)$ is $1$, and $\chi_E(x) = \sum_k \chi_{E_k}(x)$. Hence $f\chi_E = \sum_k f\chi_{E_k}$ pointwise: if $x \in E_j$ both sides equal $f(x)$ (the only nonzero term is the $j$-th, also when $f(x) = \infty$), and if $x \notin E$ both sides are $0$. By term-by-term integration of nonnegative series, $\int f\chi_E = \sum_k \int f\chi_{E_k}$.

(b) The functions $f\chi_{E_k}$ are measurable, increase with $k$ because the $E_k$ do, and converge pointwise to $f\chi_E$: a point of $E$ lies in $E_k$ for all large $k$, and a point outside $E$ gives $0$ throughout. The monotone convergence theorem gives $\int f\chi_{E_k} \to \int f\chi_E$.

(c) The function $f\chi_Z$ differs from the zero function only on $Z$, so $f\chi_Z = 0$ almost everywhere. Zero sets do not affect integrals, so $\int f\chi_Z = \int 0 = m(\emptyset) = 0$.
hints: $f\chi_E = \sum_k f\chi_{E_k}$ pointwise; integrate term by term. For (b) use monotone convergence, and for (c) the fact that integrals ignore zero sets.

blocks.title: Absolute continuity of the integral
blocks.tex:
Let $f : \R^n \to [0, \infty]$ be measurable with $\int f < \infty$. Show that for every $\eps > 0$ there is a $\delta > 0$ such that
\[ \int_E f < \eps \qquad \text{for every measurable } E \subseteq \R^n \text{ with } mE < \delta, \]
where $\int_E f = \int f\chi_E$.
blocks.proof:
For $k \in \N$ let $g_k = \min(f, k)$ and let $r_k$ be the excess, $r_k(x) = f(x) - k$ if $f(x) > k$ (with $\infty - k = \infty$) and $r_k(x) = 0$ otherwise. Both are measurable by the theorem on superlevel sets: for $a \ge 0$, $\set{g_k > a}$ is $\set{f > a}$ if $a < k$ and empty if $a \ge k$, and $\set{r_k > a} = \set{f > a + k}$. Moreover $f = g_k + r_k$ pointwise: if $f(x) \le k$ the right side is $f(x) + 0$, and if $f(x) > k$ it is $k + (f(x) - k) = f(x)$, also when $f(x) = \infty$.

By additivity, $\int f = \int g_k + \int r_k$, and all three integrals are finite. The functions $g_k$ increase pointwise to $f$ (once $k \ge f(x)$ they equal $f(x)$, and if $f(x) = \infty$ they equal $k$), so the monotone convergence theorem gives $\int g_k \to \int f$, hence $\int r_k = \int f - \int g_k \to 0$. Fix $k$ with $\int r_k < \eps/2$ and put $\delta = \eps/(2k)$.

Now let $E$ be measurable with $mE < \delta$. The functions $g_k\chi_E$ and $r_k\chi_E$ are measurable (their superlevel sets are those of $g_k$ and $r_k$ intersected with $E$), and $f\chi_E = g_k\chi_E + r_k\chi_E$. By additivity and monotonicity of the integral, since $g_k\chi_E \le k\chi_E$ and $r_k\chi_E \le r_k$,
\[ \int_E f = \int g_k\chi_E + \int r_k\chi_E \le \int k\chi_E + \int r_k = k\, mE + \int r_k < k\delta + \frac{\eps}{2} = \eps . \]
hints: Split $f$ into the bounded part $\min(f, k)$ and the excess $f - \min(f, k)$. The excess has small integral once $k$ is large, by monotone convergence and additivity.
On a set of measure less than $\delta$, the bounded part contributes at most $k\delta$.

blocks.title: The graph of a measurable function is a zero set
blocks.tex:
Let $f : \R^n \to [0, \infty]$ be measurable. Show that its graph
\[ \Gamma = \set{ (x, f(x)) : x \in \R^n, \ f(x) < \infty } \]
is a zero set in $\R^{n+1}$.
blocks.proof:
\emph{Step 1: finite-valued functions of finite integral.} Let $g : \R^n \to [0, \infty)$ be measurable with $\int g < \infty$, and let $\Gamma_g = \set{(x, g(x)) : x \in \R^n}$. We claim $\Gamma_g = \widehat{\mathcal{U}}g \setminus \mathcal{U}g$. A point $(x, y)$ lies in $\widehat{\mathcal{U}}g$ but not in $\mathcal{U}g$ exactly when $0 \le y \le g(x)$ and not $y < g(x)$, that is, when $y = g(x)$; conversely $(x, g(x))$ satisfies $0 \le g(x) \le g(x)$ and not $g(x) < g(x)$. By the proposition on the completed undergraph, both $\widehat{\mathcal{U}}g$ and $\mathcal{U}g$ are measurable with $m(\widehat{\mathcal{U}}g) = \int g = m(\mathcal{U}g) < \infty$, and $\mathcal{U}g \subseteq \widehat{\mathcal{U}}g$. Hence $\Gamma_g$ is measurable and
\[ m\Gamma_g = m(\widehat{\mathcal{U}}g) - m(\mathcal{U}g) = 0 . \]

\emph{Step 2: the general case.} Let $f_k = \min(f, k)\chi_{C_k}$ with $C_k = [-k,k]^n$ be the truncations of the exercise on truncation: each $f_k$ is measurable, takes values in $[0, k]$, and has finite integral. By Step 1 each graph $\Gamma_{f_k}$ is a zero set. If $f(x) < \infty$, choose $k$ so large that $x \in C_k$ and $k \ge f(x)$; then $f_k(x) = f(x)$, so $(x, f(x)) \in \Gamma_{f_k}$. Therefore $\Gamma \subseteq \bigcup_k \Gamma_{f_k}$, a countable union of zero sets, and $\Gamma$ is a zero set.
hints: The graph is the difference between the completed undergraph and the undergraph, two measurable sets with the same measure.
If $\int f = \infty$ the subtraction is illegal: truncate $f$ first (an earlier exercise), and take a countable union of graphs.

blocks.title: Dominated convergence from Fatou's lemma
blocks.tex:
Let $f_k, g : \R^n \to [0, \infty]$ be measurable with $f_k \le g$ for all $k$ and $\int g < \infty$.

(a) Show the reverse Fatou inequality $\displaystyle \limsup_{k \to \infty} \int f_k \le \int \limsup_{k \to \infty} f_k$.

(b) Deduce the dominated convergence theorem: if $f_k(x) \to f(x)$ for every $x$, then $\int f_k \to \int f$.
blocks.proof:
(a) \emph{Making $g$ finite.} The set $Z = \set{g = \infty}$ is a zero set by Chebyshev's inequality (part (c)), and it is measurable. Put $g' = g\chi_{Z^c}$ and $f_k' = f_k\chi_{Z^c}$. These are measurable (their superlevel sets are $\set{g > a} \cap Z^c$ and $\set{f_k > a} \cap Z^c$), finite-valued, satisfy $f_k' \le g'$, and agree with $g$ and $f_k$ almost everywhere, so $\int g' = \int g$ and $\int f_k' = \int f_k$ because zero sets do not affect integrals. Also $\limsup_k f_k' = (\limsup_k f_k)\chi_{Z^c}$ agrees with $\limsup_k f_k$ almost everywhere, and $\limsup_k f_k$ is measurable, so $\int \limsup_k f_k' = \int \limsup_k f_k$. Thus it suffices to prove (a) for the primed functions, and we may assume that $g$, hence every $f_k$ and $F = \limsup_k f_k$, takes only finite values. Note $F \le g$ and $F$ is measurable.

\emph{Fatou for the differences.} The functions $g - f_k$ and $g - F$ take values in $[0, \infty)$. They are measurable: as real-valued functions, $g$, $f_k$ and $F$ are measurable in the sense of the lemma on real-valued functions (their positive parts are themselves and their negative parts vanish), so $g - f_k = g + (-1) f_k$ and $g - F$ are measurable by that lemma, and being nonnegative they coincide with their positive parts. For each $x$, since $g(x)$ is finite and $0 \le f_k(x) \le g(x)$,
\[ \liminf_{k} \bigl( g(x) - f_k(x) \bigr) = g(x) - \limsup_k f_k(x) = g(x) - F(x). \]
Fatou's lemma applied to the sequence $g - f_k$ gives
\[ \int (g - F) \le \liminf_{k} \int (g - f_k). \]
By additivity, $\int g = \int (g - F) + \int F$ and $\int g = \int (g - f_k) + \int f_k$, and all these integrals are at most $\int g < \infty$ by monotonicity. Substituting,
\[ \int g - \int F \le \liminf_k \Bigl( \int g - \int f_k \Bigr) = \int g - \limsup_k \int f_k, \]
and since $\int g$ is finite, $\limsup_k \int f_k \le \int F = \int \limsup_k f_k$.

(b) If $f_k \to f$ pointwise, then $f = \liminf_k f_k = \limsup_k f_k$, and $f$ is measurable. Fatou's lemma gives $\int f \le \liminf_k \int f_k$, and (a) gives $\limsup_k \int f_k \le \int f$. Hence $\liminf_k \int f_k = \limsup_k \int f_k = \int f$, that is, $\int f_k \to \int f$.
hints: Fatou's lemma bounds a lower limit from below. To bound an upper limit from above, feed it a sequence that goes the other way: subtract $f_k$ from something.

Apply Fatou's lemma to the nonnegative functions $g - f_k$. First arrange that $g$ is finite everywhere: it is finite almost everywhere, and changing functions on a zero set changes no integral. Then $\liminf_k (g - f_k) = g - \limsup_k f_k$ pointwise, and all integrals are finite, so you may subtract.

blocks.title: A convergent improper integral of a nonnegative function is a Lebesgue integral
blocks.tex:
Let $f : [0, \infty) \to [0, \infty)$ be continuous and suppose that the improper Riemann integral converges: the limit
\[ \lim_{b \to \infty} \int_0^b f \]
of the Riemann integrals over $[0,b]$ exists and is finite. Extend $f$ to $\R$ by $f(x) = 0$ for $x < 0$. Show that $f$ is Lebesgue integrable and that its Lebesgue integral equals $\lim_{b \to \infty} \int_0^b f$. (A continuous function on a closed bounded interval is Riemann integrable, by Chapter 3.)
blocks.proof:
For $k \in \N$ let $f_k = f\chi_{[0,k]}$. The restriction of $f$ to $[0,k]$ is continuous, hence Riemann integrable, and $f_k$ is that restriction extended by $0$ outside $[0,k]$. By the theorem that Riemann integrable functions are Lebesgue integrable, $f_k$ is Lebesgue measurable and its Lebesgue integral equals the Riemann integral $\int_0^k f$.

Since $f \ge 0$, the functions $f_k$ increase with $k$, and $f_k(x) \to f(x)$ for every $x$: for $x \ge 0$ we have $f_k(x) = f(x)$ as soon as $k \ge x$, and for $x < 0$ everything is $0$. By the monotone convergence theorem, $f$ is Lebesgue measurable and
\[ \int f = \lim_{k \to \infty} \int f_k = \lim_{k \to \infty} \int_0^k f = \lim_{b \to \infty} \int_0^b f , \]
the last step because a limit as $b \to \infty$ that exists is also the limit along the integers $b = k$. The right side is finite, so $f$ is integrable.
hints: Apply monotone convergence to $f\chi_{[0,k]}$, each of which is Riemann integrable on $[0,k]$.
